_Why can a better prediction still produce a worse physical action?_

A learned model can recognize a task correctly and still act too late to stop a moving machine or prevent excessive contact force. Once a command produces motion or heat, replacing the prediction cannot undo the work already delivered. The engineer must therefore connect model quality to the body's limits, the time available to respond, and the evidence supporting the next action. An independent permission path must be able to refuse a proposal and carry out a feasible fallback even when the model stalls. At the causal boundary, where commands become physical work, irreversibility makes these responsibilities part of the system's architecture.

- Apply the scope test to distinguish physical AI from advisory learning and classical control

## Artificial Intelligence Beyond Glass {#sec-boundary-beyond-glass}

Most machine learning systems deliver an output that a person or another program acts on, such as a ranking, a label, or a paragraph of text. The discipline that engineers them, from data collection and training compute to evaluation and deployment, matured around such predictions. Physical AI systems are machine learning systems whose outputs are physical actions. A learned model's output becomes a setpoint, the setpoint becomes current in a motor winding, and the current becomes force and motion in a body that shares space with people and objects. That chain moves the unit of engineering from the prediction to the action, and it changes what an error costs. A wrong answer on a screen can be discarded, but a command that has already moved a machine can be answered only by another physical action, which takes time and must itself be feasible. The interface where a command becomes physical work is the causal boundary, and the irreversibility of what crosses it is the constraint this book is organized around.

Physical AI did not arrive with large models. It is the latest stage of an evolution in which two older lines of engineering converged. Robotics and control learned to act on a world that pushes back, and machine learning learned to predict from data at scale. Over nearly eighty years the learned model has moved, one step at a time, from the edge of the machine toward its actuators, and each step changed what the rest of the machine had to guarantee. That history explains what physical AI inherits and why its central engineering problem is nonetheless new.

### From prediction to action {#sec-boundary-prediction-to-action}

The acting line begins with feedback. Wiener's cybernetics described animals and machines alike as systems that measure the result of their own action and use it to correct the next one [@wiener1948cybernetics], and control theory soon learned to estimate a moving system's state from noisy measurements [@kalman1960new]. The first industrial robots needed little of this at the level of the task. In 1961 a Unimate arm began stacking hot die-cast parts at General Motors by replaying step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum [@chm1961unimate]. Nothing in that program could notice a person in the arm's path, so protecting people meant keeping them out of its reach. The machine acted, but it did not perceive, and nothing in it was learned. @Fig-01-evolution places this and the later milestones on the two lines and marks where they converge.

::: {#fig-01-evolution fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**From prediction to action**: Robotics and control (top) learned to act on the physical world, and machine learning (bottom) learned to predict from data; the two lines merge in learned action. The band beneath the time axis shows where the learned output lands in typical deployed systems of each era, from no learned component, to learned perception feeding hand-written planners, to learned motor commands, to pretrained models that propose motion. The time axis widens after 2005." fig-alt="Timeline from the late 1940s to 2026 with two horizontal lanes that merge. The upper lane, robotics and control, learning to act, marks cybernetics 1948, Unimate 1961, Shakey 1966 to 1972, subsumption 1986, probabilistic robotics from the 1990s to 2005, and the Grand Challenge 2005. The lower lane, machine learning, learning to predict, marks ALVINN 1989 and deep networks on ImageNet 2012. Around 2015 both lanes curve into one thicker lane labeled learned action, marking visuomotor policies 2016, chunked and diffusion policies 2023, and VLA models 2023 to 2025, ending in an arrow. The time axis widens after 2005. A band beneath the axis, labeled where the learned output lands in typical deployed systems, reads nothing learned until the mid 1980s, then learned perception feeds hand-written planners until about 2015, then learned motor commands, then pretrained proposers."}
![](images/svg/fig01_evolution.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Shakey, developed at SRI from 1966 through 1972, joined perception to planning [@nilsson1984shakey]. It took camera images and range-finder readings, kept a model of its surroundings, and used a planner called STRIPS to compose sequences of actions that would achieve a stated goal. This organization, later summarized as sense-plan-act (@sec-appendix-spa), treats acting as the last step of a computation. Shakey moved very slowly, and its designers treated its motion as running asynchronously to the programs directing it [@nilsson1984shakey]; the world was assumed to wait while the computer thought. Shakey also carried a detail that anticipates this book's architecture. When one of its catwhiskers touched an obstacle, the robot stopped by a reflex action beneath the planner.

Brooks inverted that organization. His subsumption architecture built control from layers of simple, asynchronous behaviors, each coupling sensing to action. Higher layers could suppress the outputs of lower ones, but the lower layers continued to run as higher ones were added [@brooks1986robust]. A fast layer that keeps working while a slow one is busy or wrong is an ancestor of the permission path this book develops. The difficulty every approach faced had a name. **Moravec's paradox**\index{Moravec's paradox}[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox] [@moravec1988mind] observes that sensorimotor skills people perform with little conscious effort can be difficult to reproduce computationally, which is why learning became attractive for physical tasks.

[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox]: **Moravec's Paradox**\index{Moravec's Paradox}: The observation in artificial intelligence [@moravec1988mind] that high-level reasoning requires comparatively little computation, whereas low-level sensorimotor coordination demands enormous perceptual and computational resources.

Learning had already entered the loop. In 1989 ALVINN, a small neural network, mapped camera and laser range images to the direction a vehicle should steer, and followed real roads under some field conditions [@pomerleau1989alvinn]; @sec-data-collection-sources returns to it. Through the 1990s robotics also made uncertainty explicit. Probabilistic robotics represents what a machine believes about itself and its surroundings as probability distributions, updated as actions and measurements arrive [@thrun2005probabilistic]. The DARPA Grand Challenge tested these ideas at scale. In the first race, in 2004, no vehicle covered more than a small fraction of the desert course. In 2005 five vehicles finished, and the winner, Stanford's Stanley, relied predominantly on machine learning and probabilistic reasoning [@thrun2006stanley]. In systems of this kind, learning mostly estimated what the world was like, and hand-written planners and controllers decided what to do. A decade later, the DARPA Robotics Challenge Finals asked robots to work at a simulated disaster site, driving a vehicle, opening a door, turning a valve, and climbing stairs. The organizers deliberately degraded the communications link to the remote human operators, so that each robot had to carry out parts of every task under supervised autonomy rather than direct teleoperation [@krotkov2017darpa]. Even at that stage, a person remained close to the loop.

Deep learning then changed how much a machine could perceive. In 2012 a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs classified ImageNet photographs with error well below the previous state of the art [@krizhevsky2012imagenet], and learned detectors spread into the perception systems of robots and automated vehicles. The architecture around them usually stayed modular, with a learned percept feeding a planner written as rules or as an optimization. The learned outputs were still predictions, yet no person stood between them and the brakes. The Tempe vehicle examined in @sec-boundary-when-fails was a machine of this kind.

Learning reached the actuator itself in the following years. Levine and colleagues trained convolutional networks that mapped raw camera images directly to the torques at a robot's motors, for tasks such as screwing a cap onto a bottle [@levine2016endtoend]. Grasping systems learned from hundreds of thousands of their own attempts, gathered by groups of robot arms working in parallel [@levine2018learning; @kalashnikov2018qtopt], and deep reinforcement learning in simulation produced controllers for a legged robot and a dexterous hand that transferred to hardware [@hwangbo2019learning; @akkaya2019solving]. With that step the data changed character. A robot that learns from its own attempts chooses the states it will see, so its training data depends on its own behavior.

Imitation learning made human demonstration a practical route to new manipulation skills, and two ideas shaped the policies now in use. Action chunking predicts a short sequence of future actions from each observation, a design its authors motivated partly by the way a cloned policy's errors compound over time [@zhao2023learning]. Diffusion policies generate action sequences by iterative denoising, which lets one policy represent the several different ways a demonstrator might complete the same task [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The learned output had become a short plan of future motion, executed by controllers beneath it.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-vla-state
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ROBOT FOUNDATION MODELS, STATE OF PRACTICE AS OF 2026 (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-vla-state in @sec-boundary-prediction-to-action.
# │ Goal:    Record the rate structure each system's authors report, so the
# │          table can be refreshed for a later edition without touching prose.
# │ Show:    OpenVLA 7B params, 970k demos, about 6 Hz on one desktop GPU;
# │          pi0 chunks up to 50 Hz; GR00T N1 10 Hz reasoning and 120 Hz
# │          actions; Gemini Robotics under 160 ms backbone, about 250 ms
# │          end to end, 50 Hz effective control.
# │ How:     Values are the papers' own reported figures (category: literature),
# │          loaded here until the literature registry holds them.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

class VLAState:
    """Rates and sizes reported by the authors of representative robot foundation models."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. Kim et al. (2024), arXiv:2406.09246, abstract and Sec. 3
    openvla_params_b = 7  # billion parameters
    openvla_demos_k = 970  # thousand real-robot demonstrations
    openvla_rate = 6 * hertz  # about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090, bfloat16, no compilation
    # category: literature. Black et al. (2024), arXiv:2410.24164, Sec. I
    pi0_chunk_rate = 50 * hertz  # action chunks at up to 50 Hz
    # category: literature. NVIDIA (2025), arXiv:2503.14734, Sec. 1
    groot_s2_rate = 10 * hertz  # System 2 vision-language module on an L40
    groot_s1_rate = 120 * hertz  # System 1 action module
    # category: literature. Gemini Robotics Team (2025), arXiv:2503.20020, Sec. 3.1
    gemini_backbone_latency = 160 * millisecond  # cloud backbone, query to response (upper bound)
    gemini_e2e_latency = 250 * millisecond  # observation to action chunk, approximate
    gemini_control_rate = 50 * hertz  # effective control frequency with chunking

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Nothing is derived; the table reports each paper's own figures.

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(groot_s1_rate > groot_s2_rate, "GR00T N1's action module must run faster than its reasoning module.")
    check(gemini_e2e_latency > gemini_backbone_latency, "End-to-end latency includes the backbone.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    openvla_params_str = fmt_int(openvla_params_b)
    openvla_demos_str = fmt_int(openvla_demos_k)
    openvla_rate_str = fmt_frequency(openvla_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    pi0_chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(pi0_chunk_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    groot_s2_rate_str = fmt_frequency(groot_s2_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    groot_s1_rate_str = fmt_frequency(groot_s1_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    gemini_backbone_str = fmt_latency(gemini_backbone_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gemini_e2e_str = fmt_latency(gemini_e2e_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    gemini_rate_str = fmt_frequency(gemini_control_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

The latest step changed where learned proposals come from. Large multitask datasets collected on many robots prepared the ground [@brohan2023rt1; @open_x_embodiment_collaboration2024open], and between 2023 and 2025 several groups showed that a model pretrained on web-scale images and text can be fine-tuned to emit robot actions directly. These **vision-language-action (VLA) models**\index{Vision-language-action model} share one mechanism. A pretrained vision-language backbone encodes the camera images and an instruction, and an action head converts the backbone's output into motor commands. The head either decodes actions as discrete tokens, the way a language model decodes words [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], or produces a continuous *action chunk*, a short sequence of future setpoints from one inference [@black2024pi0]. A backbone with billions of parameters cannot run at a controller's rate, so recent designs split the work across rates: a slow model interprets the scene and a fast action model or on-robot decoder emits chunks that controllers execute [@bjorck2025gr00t; @geminirobotics2025]. @Tbl-01-vla-state records what their authors report. The running machine adopts the same hierarchy, with an intent model and a chunk policy at the rates fixed on its card in @sec-boundary-running-machine, and @sec-brain develops the costs. The consequence for this book is direct. A general-purpose learned model can now propose motion for a general-purpose machine, so deciding which component may *permit* that motion becomes a design question for every machine that adopts one.

| OpenVLA (2024) [@kim2024openvla]             | Each action dimension discretized into a token; `{python} VLAState.openvla_params_str` billion parameters, trained on `{python} VLAState.openvla_demos_str` thousand robot demonstrations | One model; about `{python} VLAState.openvla_rate_str` on one desktop GPU                                                                                                                                  |
| $\pi_0$ (2024) [@black2024pi0]               | Continuous action chunks from a flow-matching action expert attached to the backbone                                                                                                      | Chunks executed at up to `{python} VLAState.pi0_chunk_rate_str`                                                                                                                                           |
| GR00T N1 (2025) [@bjorck2025gr00t]           | Vision-language module (System 2) conditions a diffusion-transformer action module (System 1)                                                                                             | Reasoning at `{python} VLAState.groot_s2_rate_str`, actions at `{python} VLAState.groot_s1_rate_str`                                                                                                      |
| Gemini Robotics (2025) [@geminirobotics2025] | Cloud-hosted VLA backbone and an action decoder on the robot's computer                                                                                                                   | Backbone under `{python} VLAState.gemini_backbone_str`; about `{python} VLAState.gemini_e2e_str` from observation to action chunk; `{python} VLAState.gemini_rate_str` effective control through chunking |

The mechanisms (pretrained backbone, action head, chunking across rates) are durable; the named systems are dated instances that a later edition should refresh. Rates depend on the reported hardware and are not comparable across rows. {#tbl-01-vla-state tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

The name *physical AI* is recent, and industry usage since 2024 applies it broadly to almost any AI that perceives and acts in the physical world [@nvidia2026physicalai]. The history above runs through two research traditions that cover much of the same ground. **Embodied AI**\index{Embodied AI} descends from Brooks's argument that intelligent behavior arises from a body situated in and interacting with its environment rather than from abstract representation alone [@brooks1991intelligence]. **Cyber-physical systems**\index{Cyber-physical systems} name the integration of computation and networking with physical processes, and they carry the timing and verification discipline of embedded engineering [@leeseshia2017embedded]. Embodied AI supplies much of the learning this book uses, and cyber-physical systems supply much of its timing and verification practice. The book's subject is where the two meet at an actuator, and the definition at the end of this section is deliberately narrower than industry usage: the scope test in @sec-boundary-scope-test makes it testable.

Read as one story, this history moves the learned model step by step toward the actuator. At first nothing was learned. Then learned percepts fed hand-written planners, learned policies emitted motor commands, and finally pretrained general-purpose models began to propose motion for many kinds of machine. At each step, a guarantee that separation or human inspection used to supply had to move inside the machine. The familiar concerns of machine learning systems engineering come along, and each acquires physical stakes. Data stops being a fixed corpus, because the machine's own actions choose what it will observe next. Compute stops being a matter of throughput and cost alone, because a late answer is paid for in stopping distance. Evaluation stops being a score on held-out examples, because competence that matters is shown only in the closed loop. Deployment stops being a version rollout, because a release grants a machine authority over motion near people. When a learned output becomes an irreversible action, none of these concerns can be settled inside the model. They belong to the whole machine, and they meet at the boundary where its commands become physical work.

### The question this book answers {#sec-boundary-central-question}

That convergence is why the problem now faces the whole field rather than a few robotics specialists. The central question of this book is why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action, and what the rest of the machine must supply so that a learned proposal becomes useful work within justified limits. The book's answer is an argument in four steps. The body's physical limits bound what any proposal may ask for. The learned proposer's competence holds only over the states its data and evaluation covered, and its own actions choose those states. An independent permission path, not the model, decides what may execute. The evidence gathered about the whole machine bounds the conditions under which it may operate. This chapter establishes the vocabulary of that argument: the causal boundary and the cost of delay at it, the scope of physical AI, a five-level model of the machine that separates proposal from permission, and the four laws that organize the rest of the book.

One machine carries the argument through every chapter. A warehouse mobile manipulator must collect an object from a conveyor, open a spring-latched cage door, and carry its load through an aisle shared with people. These tasks join abilities often studied separately. The machine must recognize an unfamiliar object, choose a grasp, coordinate its arm and base, and respond when contact or the scene differs from expectation. Learning makes varied behavior possible; engineering must turn that behavior into useful, repeatable physical work.

This book develops the ability to design, teach, integrate, evaluate, and maintain such a machine within justified operating limits. Its recurring warehouse machine is an illustrative engineering design, not a report of a qualified deployment. The same task connects physical budgets, learning experiments, runtime decisions, and evidence for service. When the evidence is incomplete, the engineer must identify what measurement, new experience, or design change would support the next capability.

Consider the base approaching the end of a storage rack while its model processes a camera image. A worker steps into the aisle before the next proposal returns. The computer can still discard that proposal, but the robot has continued moving throughout the calculation. Choosing an action requires reasoning about both the prediction and the physical state in which it will execute.

Restoring a software state cannot restore the position of a moving robot or repair an object it has struck. The physical plant, the apparatus being controlled such as the robot's wheeled base or arm, changes state while the computer calculates. The model must recognize a useful action, the execution mechanism must judge it while the observation remains relevant, and the body must be able to deliver the admitted motion or a feasible alternative. A stronger prediction alone cannot recover clearance already consumed during computation, so the engineering problem leads from physical limits to the architecture that checks each proposed action.

Building such a machine requires contributions from several disciplines. Machine learning supplies perception and action proposals. Computer systems determine how quickly the computation and communication finish, including the limits imposed by memory traffic [@williams2009roofline]. Mechanics and control establish which motions the plant can sustain. Embedded systems enforce the timing and access rules that connect a proposal to an actuator. These responsibilities meet at a common decision: whether the proposed action can execute under the machine's current conditions. This book develops the reasoning needed to make and justify that decision.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The separation of learned proposals from actuation authority is mapped to isolated silicon domains in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#dfn-boundary-physical-artificial-intelligence-physical-ai .callout-definition title="Physical artificial intelligence"}

***Physical artificial intelligence***\index{Physical Artificial Intelligence!definition}\index{Physical AI!definition} is the engineering of closed-loop machines in which learned models influence, without synchronous human approval, physical actions that change subsequent observations.

1.  **Significance**: Model performance becomes a property of an operating machine. Its actions must fit the plant's physical limits and the time available to respond.
2.  **Distinction**: The scope test later in this chapter combines a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated physical authority. Neither a model used only for advice nor an automated machine without a learned component meets all three criteria.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the body as a peripheral device for a model. A useful proposal still needs an independent permission decision based on the current state, physical limits, and available fallback.

:::

The argument starts where the definition does, with the difference between a proposed action and its physical effect. A short stopping calculation then puts a number on what delay costs at the causal boundary, and a documented collision later in the chapter shows these responsibilities failing together before four laws distill them.

## Defining the Cyber-Physical Causal Boundary {#sec-boundary-causal-boundary}

An advisory model that displays an inference result on a screen or returns a JSON payload to a web client has no direct electrical or mechanical coupling to physical actuators. A human operator or downstream software can inspect and discard the prediction before anything acts on it. That does not make digital errors benign, since an operator may still act on a flawed recommendation. The relevant distinction is whether the automated system can turn an accepted model proposal into physical action. Arbitration belongs inside that system; it protects the causal boundary rather than removing it.

### From a proposed action to motion {#sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon}

In modern computational frameworks, executing `action_chunk = policy(observation)` produces a floating-point tensor. The tensor describes a proposed action; moving the machine requires a chain of controllers and physical actuators. The causal boundary is the interface through which an admitted command changes the physical plant.

A learned policy can propose a sequence of future positions or velocities. Those numbers remain a description of motion until a controller accepts and executes them. The representation and useful duration of such sequences are developed in @sec-brain; here the distinction is between describing an action and authorizing its consequences.

The permission path, an independent mechanism that alone may let a proposal reach the drives (defined in @sec-boundary-machine-model), checks whether the proposed motion fits the current physical limits and can be carried out in time. If admitted, its setpoints pass to the controllers that drive the motors. A position controller determines the motion correction needed; the drive regulates electrical current to produce torque. @Sec-body develops the physical limits of this conversion, and @sec-nervous develops its timing and authority boundaries.

For a motor driven by pulse-width modulation (PWM), a software write sets a hardware timer's switching command. The power electronics use that signal to control current in the motor windings. Electromagnetic torque then accelerates the rotor and attached mechanism. This example establishes the distinction needed here: changing a proposed setpoint in memory is different from changing a command that has already produced motion. A later command can brake or redirect the machine, but that response takes time and must itself remain physically feasible.

::: {#dfn-boundary-causal-boundary .callout-definition title="Causal boundary"}

***Causal boundary***\index{Causal boundary!definition} is the interface through which a digital command produces physical forces, currents, or flows.

1.  **Significance**: A proposal can be rejected before it changes the plant. Once executed, it can alter the environment, dissipate energy, and change subsequent observations.
2.  **Distinction**: Restoring a command in memory does not restore the machine's prior physical state. Recovery requires another physical action, with its own limits and consequences.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming that canceling a software task stops the motion it initiated. The machine needs a feasible stopping or holding response even when its proposer stops computing.

:::

An offline test can hold its examples fixed regardless of the model's predictions. A robot cannot generally rely on that separation: turning the chassis changes the next camera view, pushing an object changes its location, and the warehouse base's movement changes both its distance from the worker and the next image available to its model. The feedback loop with which the history in @sec-boundary-prediction-to-action began now applies to the learned model itself. A machine that acts changes the conditions of its next observation, so the learning problem must account for observations that depend on earlier actions.

In a physical system, the environment evolves in a closed causal loop: the next physical state $\mathbf{s}_{t+1}$ and incoming sensor observation $\mathbf{o}_{t+1}$ depend directly on the action $\mathbf{a}_t$ produced by the prior model inference. The sensory input stream is endogenous, governed by closed-loop dynamics, represented here at successive observation times:
$$\mathbf{s}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t), \quad \mathbf{o}_{t+1} \sim p(\mathbf{o} \mid \mathbf{s}_{t+1})$$
Here $\mathbf{f}$ is the plant's dynamics, written without process noise for this introduction, and $p$ is the observation model that turns a physical state into a sensor reading.

An erroneous action can therefore move the machine into states poorly represented in its training data. Errors in those states may produce further departures from the demonstrated behavior (@fig-01-causal-loop). Imitation learning calls this **covariate shift**\index{Covariate shift!closed loop}: a policy trained on the states an expert visited is deployed on the states its own actions produce, and the expected cost of its mistakes can grow with the square of the task horizon rather than linearly [@ross2011reduction]. @Sec-data-covariate-shift develops the mechanism. This possibility motivates closed-loop evaluation; it does not mean that every error necessarily produces an unstable trajectory.

::: {#fig-01-causal-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The closed causal loop**: Advisory output (top) stops at an informational interface. In physical AI (bottom), permitted model proposals reach hardware registers, where electrical current produces force and motion. Those actions alter the environment and subsequent sensor observations." fig-alt="Flowchart contrasting advisory predictions with physical AI. The upper path ends at an informational interface; the lower path carries sensor observations to a proposal, the permission path, motor actuators, and a changing physical plant."}
