### Delay consumes stopping clearance {#sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline}

A moving base needs distance both before braking begins and while braking brings it to rest. For a steady initial speed, constant deceleration after onset, and a stationary obstacle, the elementary stopping budget is:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = \underbrace{v \tau_{\text{delay}}}_{\text{travel during response delay}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}}}_{\text{mechanical dissipation}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$$
Here $v$ is the initial speed (m/s), $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ is the full interval (s) from the relevant observation to the onset of retarding force, $a_{\text{brake}}$ is the braking deceleration (m/s²) assumed for this calculation, and $D_{\text{clear}}$ is the usable observed clearance (m). The first term is travel during the delay; the second is travel while shedding kinetic energy. Setting $v \tau_{\text{delay}} = v^2/(2 a_{\text{brake}})$ and dividing by $v$ shows that the two terms are equal at the crossover speed $v^{*} = 2 a_{\text{brake}} \tau_{\text{delay}}$. Below $v^{*}$ the delay dominates the stop; above it braking dominates, and because braking grows with the square of speed, slowing down pays off faster than shortening the delay (@fig-01-kinematic-roofline). Solving the inequality for $v$ gives the fastest speed the clearance allows, which @sec-body-kinetic-momentum derives.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-stopping-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S ELEMENTARY STOPPING BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-boundary-stopping-budget in @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Goal:    Close the stopping inequality against the card's clear distance,
# │          open the pre-brake delay into its registry terms, and show the
# │          crossover speed and a half-speed what-if.
# │ Show:    133.6 ms = 51.6 + 60 + 1 + 1 + 20 ms; 200.4 + 562.5 = 762.9 mm
# │          inside 1.10 m (337.1 mm spare); v* = 0.53 m/s; backbone 22 ms is
# │          33 mm; at 0.75 m/s the stop is 240.8 mm. Guard: the finished
# │          budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget exceeds D_clear at the
# │          drive limit, which the prose states without printing it.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE fields from the warehouse mobile manipulator in mlsysim;
# │          the guard reuses calc_c2_stop_suffix and calc_scurve_stop_distance
# │          exactly as @sec-enforcement-composite-budget does. No value is retyped.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class StoppingBudget:
    """Elementary stopping budget of the loaded base at its drive limit (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (aisle speed on the card)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (mid-exposure to proposer dispatch)
    t_backbone = AISLE.t_backbone  # category: illustrative (perception backbone, inside t_age)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen (chunk lease)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (one permission tick)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (one bus cycle)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative (brake command to retarding force)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (sum of the five terms above)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_sum = (t_age + t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_onset).to(millisecond)
    blind = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    d_stop = (blind + d_brake).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - d_stop).to(millimeter)
    blind_share = (blind / d_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    brake_over_blind = (d_brake / blind).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    v_star = (2 * a_brake * tau_delay).to(meter / second)
    d_backbone = (v * t_backbone).to(millimeter)
    d_lease = (v * t_lease).to(millimeter)
    d_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    v_half = v / 2
    blind_half = (v_half * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    brake_half = (v_half**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    d_stop_half = (blind_half + brake_half).to(millimeter)
    # Guard only: the finished budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget at the drive limit
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    d_finished = (calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake) + blind + AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.delta_margin + AISLE.eps_track).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_sum.magnitude - tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "tau_delay must equal its five registry terms.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, f"Canon tau_delay is 133.6 ms, got {tau_delay}.")
    check(abs(d_stop.magnitude - 762.9) < 5e-3, f"Canon elementary stop is 762.9 mm, got {d_stop}.")
    check(spare.magnitude > 0, "The elementary budget must fit inside D_clear at the drive limit.")
    check(v_star < v, "At the drive limit braking, not delay, must dominate.")
    check(d_finished > d_clear, "Prose says the finished budget exceeds D_clear at the drive limit.")
    check(v_aisle < v, "Prose says the aisle speed sits below the drive limit.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(t_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    blind_share_str = fmt_percent(blind_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    brake_over_blind_mult_str = fmt_multiple(brake_over_blind, precision=1)
    d_backbone_str = fmt_length(d_backbone, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_lease_str = fmt_length(d_lease, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_per_ms_str = fmt_length(d_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_half_str = fmt_velocity(v_half, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    d_stop_half_str = fmt_length(d_stop_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    blind_half_str = fmt_length(blind_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    brake_half_str = fmt_length(brake_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)

    _v = fmt(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    _a = fmt(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    _tau_s = fmt(tau_delay, unit=second, precision=4)
    _blind = fmt(blind, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _brake = fmt(d_brake, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _stop = fmt(d_stop, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _clear = fmt(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=False)
    _spare = fmt(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _vstar = fmt(v_star, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    tau_sum_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = {fmt(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)} + {fmt(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} = {fmt(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    blind_math = fmt_display_math(rf"v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = {_v}\ \text{{m/s}} \times {_tau_s}\ \text{{s}} = {_blind}\ \text{{mm}}")
    brake_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{v^2}}{{2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({_v}\ \text{{m/s}})^2}}{{2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2}} = {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    close_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = {_blind} + {_brake} = {_stop}\ \text{{mm}} \le D_{{\text{{clear}}}} = {_clear}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad D_{{\text{{clear}}}} - d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = {_spare}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    vstar_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v^{{*}} = 2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}} \tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = 2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2 \times {_tau_s}\ \text{{s}} \approx {_vstar}\ \text{{m/s}}"
    )
```

For the illustrative warehouse base, every input comes from the machine card that @sec-boundary-running-machine collects later in this chapter, and the worked calculation below closes the inequality.

::: {#nbk-boundary-stopping-budget .callout-notebook title="Does the base stop inside its clearance?"}

**Problem**: The loaded base cruises toward a rack end at its drive limit, and a worker may step out at the end of the rack. The permission path must stop the base inside the rack-end clear distance on the machine card. Does the elementary stopping budget fit, which term dominates, and how much of the delay belongs to the learned model?

**Variables**:

* Speed $v =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str`, the drive limit (illustrative).
* Credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.a_brake_str`, loaded on a dry floor (illustrative).
* Clear distance $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` (illustrative).
* Total pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}} =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` (derived). It is the sum of five registry terms: the observation age of the camera frame that first shows the worker, `{python} StoppingBudget.t_age_str`, which includes the `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` perception backbone; the chunk lease of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_lease_str`, the longest an admitted command may drive before the permission path must act; one permission tick of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_tick_str`; one bus cycle of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_bus_str`; and a brake onset of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_onset_str`.

**Math**:

`{python} StoppingBudget.tau_sum_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.blind_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.brake_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.close_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.vstar_math`

**Result**: The elementary budget fits, with `{python} StoppingBudget.spare_str` to spare. The drive limit sits above the crossover speed, so braking dominates: it needs `{python} StoppingBudget.brake_over_blind_mult_str` the travel of the delay, and the delay adds `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_share_str` to the braking distance. At half speed, `{python} StoppingBudget.v_half_str`, delay travel halves to `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_half_str` while braking quarters to `{python} StoppingBudget.brake_half_str`, for a stop of `{python} StoppingBudget.d_stop_half_str`.

**Systems insight**: The learned model's backbone accounts for `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` of the delay, or `{python} StoppingBudget.d_backbone_str` of travel; the chunk lease alone costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_lease_str`. Each added millisecond of delay anywhere in the chain costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_per_ms_str` at this speed, so a slower but more accurate model is a distance cost the budget must absorb. The spare is not yet a safety margin. @Sec-enforcement-composite-budget adds the localization bound, a protective margin, tracking error, and the longer stop of a jerk-limited brake; together they exceed the clear distance at the drive limit, which is why the card sets the aisle speed at `{python} StoppingBudget.v_aisle_str`.

:::

::: {#fig-01-kinematic-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Delay travel and braking travel against speed**: The elementary stopping budget of the loaded base, split into travel during the `{python} StoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay, which grows linearly with speed, and braking travel at `{python} StoppingBudget.a_brake_str`, which grows with its square. The two terms are equal at the crossover speed $v^{*}$; above it braking dominates. At the `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit the elementary stop fits inside the `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance, before the allowances that later chapters add." fig-alt="Plot of distance in millimeters against speed from 0 to 2 meters per second. A straight line for travel during the delay and a rising parabola for braking travel cross at a marked crossover speed near 0.5 meters per second. Their sum rises more steeply and meets a dashed horizontal line marking the clear distance. A marked point at the drive limit of 1.5 meters per second sits on the sum curve below the line."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-01-kinematic-roofline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DELAY TRAVEL AND BRAKING TRAVEL AGAINST SPEED (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-01-kinematic-roofline in @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline
# │ Goal:    show the two terms of the elementary budget crossing at v*, and the
# │          drive-limit stop against the clear distance
# │ Show:    v tau_delay (133.6 ms), v^2/(2 a_brake) (2.0 m/s^2), their sum,
# │          D_clear 1.10 m, v* = 0.53 m/s, the 1.5 m/s point at 762.9 mm
# │ How:     StoppingBudget inputs over a speed grid; no value is retyped
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

SB = StoppingBudget
MPS = meter / second

# ┌── 1. LOAD (from boundary-stopping-budget) ─────────────────────────────────
tau = SB.tau_delay.to(second).magnitude
a = SB.a_brake.to(MPS / second).magnitude
d_clear = SB.d_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude
v_op = SB.v.to(MPS).magnitude
v_star = SB.v_star.to(MPS).magnitude
d_op = SB.d_stop.to(millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 401)
delay = v * tau * 1000.0
braking = v**2 / (2 * a) * 1000.0
total = delay + braking

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(v_op * tau * 1000.0 + v_op**2 / (2 * a) * 1000.0 - d_op) < 1e-6, "The plotted point must equal the notebook's stop.")
check(abs(v_star * tau - v_star**2 / (2 * a)) < 1e-9, "The two terms must be equal at v*.")
check(d_op < d_clear, "The drive-limit point must sit below the clear distance.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(9, 4.4))
ax.plot(v, delay, color=COLORS["BrownLine"], lw=1.8, label=r"travel during the delay, $v\,\tau_{\mathrm{delay}}$")
ax.plot(v, braking, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=1.8, label=r"braking travel, $v^2/(2a_{\mathrm{brake}})$")
ax.plot(v, total, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=2.0, label=r"elementary stop, $d_{\mathrm{stop}}$")
ax.axhline(d_clear, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (6, 3)))
ax.text(0.04, d_clear + 30, f"clear distance {d_clear / 1000:.2f} m", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.plot([v_star], [v_star * tau * 1000.0], "o", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=COLORS["primary"], mew=1.4, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"$v^*$ = {v_star:.2f} m/s",
    xy=(v_star, v_star * tau * 1000.0),
    xytext=(v_star + 0.12, 25),
    fontsize=9,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.8),
)
ax.plot([v_op], [d_op], "o", ms=7, color=COLORS["primary"], zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"drive limit {v_op:.1f} m/s: {d_op:.1f} mm",
    xy=(v_op, d_op),
    xytext=(v_op - 0.62, d_op + 170),
    fontsize=9,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.8),
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"),
)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2.0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1600)
ax.set_xlabel("Initial speed, $v$ (m/s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Distance (mm)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.93), fontsize=8.5, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

These are illustrative inputs and a derived delay, so the distances are illustrative too; none is measured stopping performance. We can change that result through several engineering decisions. Reducing response delay reduces the first term; reducing speed reduces both terms, with braking distance falling quadratically. Selecting a model only for prediction accuracy misses this physical trade-off. Yet model execution time is not automatically the braking delay. An independent protective path can respond while the learned proposer is stalled, provided its own sensing, timing, power, and fallback remain valid. Its response path, rather than the stalled model's completion time, then determines the relevant delay. Driverless industrial trucks already carry a non-learned protective path of this kind: their safety standard requires them to detect a person in their path and stop before contact [@iso3691part4]. This book adds learned proposers above such a layer and asks what the layer must know to judge them.

The calculation is deliberately incomplete as a deployment bound, and beyond the allowances the notebook lists, acceleration before braking and uncertain traction need their own. Obstacles that move matter most for the motivating scene: a worker walking toward the base closes the gap during the same delay and the same braking, which is why industrial safety distances add an approach-speed term to the machine's own stopping distance [@iso13855] (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes). @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum establishes the physical budget, and later runtime design allocates the delays within it. The introductory result is already enough to change the design question from model accuracy alone to useful behavior delivered within a physical response budget.

### Irreversibility and recovery {#sec-boundary-thermodynamic-irreversibility}

A checkpoint can restore the logical state of a computation. It cannot restore a fixture already deformed by a gripper or remove heat already dissipated in a winding. A later command can brake, release, or redirect the machine, but that recovery takes time and must itself be physically feasible. Preventive checks and recovery therefore serve different purposes.

Stopping clearance makes irreversibility visible for the mobile base. When the same machine grasps an object or holds a load, contact force and sustained energy demand can become the limiting quantities. The architecture must account for the kind of physical work the task requires.

## Three Machine Classes {#sec-boundary-three-classes}

The warehouse machine changes its limiting problem as it works. While traveling down an aisle, it needs room to stop. While pressing a door latch, it must limit contact force. While holding a load, it must supply torque without exhausting its thermal or electrical margin. These operating constraints motivate the three machine classes in @fig-01-three-archetypes.

**Mass-dominated mobility** spends stopping clearance. A mobile base, delivery vehicle, or drone carries momentum and cannot stop instantaneously. Speed, response delay, and available braking or thrust determine the room needed to change its motion.

**Contact-dominated manipulation** spends force and deformation margin. A gripper pressing against a stiff fixture can build damaging force while moving only a short distance. The useful action is still contact: opening the latch requires force. The engineering task is to deliver enough force for the task while respecting the object and mechanism's limits.

**Energy- and thermal-dominated operation** spends heat and supply margins. Holding a payload may require sustained motor current even when nothing moves. A simultaneous demand from drives and computation can also reduce the shared supply voltage. The machine must sustain the work long enough to complete its mission and preserve the resources required for its protective response.

::: {#fig-01-three-archetypes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three machine classes**: Each class is named for the constraint that dominates it and the margin it spends: (a) mass-dominated mobility (Class 1) spends stopping clearance, set by momentum and braking; (b) contact-dominated manipulation (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin, set by contact stiffness and the strength of the object and mechanism; and (c) energy- and thermal-dominated operation (Class 3) spends heat and supply margin, set by Joule heating, thermal capacitance, and power delivery. @Sec-body develops the panel equations." fig-alt="Three panels. Class 1, mass-dominated mobility: a wheeled base moving at speed v toward a rack end, with the clear distance D clear marked in red, above the relation d stop equals v tau delay plus v squared over 2 a brake. Class 2, contact-dominated manipulation: an arm whose gripper presses a spring of stiffness k c into a stiff fixture, deformation delta x and force F in red, above F approximately equals k c delta x. Class 3, energy- and thermal-dominated: power P in entering a winding of thermal capacitance C th, heat P out leaving, and a temperature bar T below a red T max line, above dT/dt equals P in minus P out over C th. Each panel names the margin it spends: stopping clearance, force and deformation margin, heat and supply margin."}
![](images/svg/fig01_three_archetypes.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The classes identify a dominant constraint, not mutually exclusive kinds of robot. Our mobile manipulator has a wheeled base, an articulated arm, navigation sensors, and a wrist camera. A learned policy can coordinate base and arm proposals [@fu2024mobile], while the assembled machine must respect all applicable limits. A fixed arm also has thermal and electrical constraints; a mobile base also encounters contact.

::: {#capstone-boundary-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="The humanoid crucible"}
A humanoid makes the coupling especially visible. Catching a load perturbs balance, a recovery step demands additional torque, and that torque draws current and generates heat. Protecting the control electronics does not by itself supply the drive energy needed for the recovery. The part-ending humanoid examples test how each engineering principle survives these coupled demands.
:::

### The running machine {#sec-boundary-running-machine}

The mobile manipulator is the one machine every later chapter works on, so its parameters are fixed once. @Tbl-01-machine-card collects the fifteen that later calculations use most, each with the evidence category defined in @sec-reader-numbers. A later worked example cites these values by name rather than restating them, and the full data sheet in @sec-appendix-systems-machine-data-sheet lists every other input with the registry field that holds it.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-machine-card
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S CARD (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-machine-card in @sec-boundary-running-machine.
# │ Goal:    Fix the fifteen parameters later chapters use most, with their
# │          evidence categories, and state the premise the credible
# │          deceleration rests on.
# │ Show:    368 kg; 1.5 and 1.3 m/s; 2.0 m/s^2 on a dry floor (mu >= 0.204 with
# │          all weight on the driven wheels, 0.250 at the load share the drive
# │          motors allow; tip-over unchecked); 7.11 m/s^3; 1.10 m; 133.6 ms;
# │          1 ms tick; 60 ms lease; 25 ms step and 50 ms replan; 336 ms intent
# │          latency at 2 Hz; 605 ms and 4.47 s takeovers.
# │ How:     machine_card() reads each row from the registry through the same
# │          helper that prints the full data sheet; the friction premise comes
# │          from calc_required_friction. Nothing is retyped here.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.embodied.datasheet import data_sheet_lookup, machine_card
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, fmt, check

class MachineCard:
    """The running machine's most-used parameters, with their evidence categories."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    card = machine_card()  # category: per row, from the registry and its provenance
    sheet = data_sheet_lookup()  # the braking premise rows of the full sheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    mu_all = sheet["mu_req"].value  # friction a_brake needs, all weight on the driven wheels
    mu_share = sheet["mu_req_rated"].value  # friction it needs at the largest allowed load share
    cg_unknown = sheet["cg_height"].value is None

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(len(card) == 15, f"The machine card prints fifteen rows, got {len(card)}.")
    check(abs(mu_all - 0.204) < 5e-4, f"Dry-floor premise is mu >= 0.204, got {mu_all}.")
    check(abs(mu_share - 0.250) < 5e-4, f"At the rated load share the premise is mu >= 0.250, got {mu_share}.")
    check(cg_unknown, "The tip-over check stays open until the loaded center of gravity is measured.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    value_str = {r.key: MarkdownStr(r.value_str) for r in card}
    category_str = {r.key: MarkdownStr(r.category_str) for r in card}
    mu_all_str = fmt(mu_all, precision=3)
    mu_share_str = fmt(mu_share, precision=3)
```

| Parameter                                   | Value                                              | Category                                              | Basis                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Loaded mass $m$                             | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["m_loaded"]`       | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["m_loaded"]`       | Base, arm, and a full tote rack; an upper bound (@sec-body-kinetic-momentum)                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Drive limit $v_{\max}$                      | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["v_drive"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["v_drive"]`        | Class profile of a warehouse base                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Aisle speed $v_{\text{aisle}}$              | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["v_aisle"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["v_aisle"]`        | Set below the dry-floor speed ceiling (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes)                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$    | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["a_brake"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["a_brake"]`        | Loaded, on a dry floor that supplies $\mu \ge$ `{python} MachineCard.mu_all_str` with all weight on the driven wheels, or `{python} MachineCard.mu_share_str` at the share the drive motors allow; tip-over is unchecked until the center of gravity is measured (@sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake) |
| Stop jerk bound $j_{\max}$                  | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["j_brake"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["j_brake"]`        | Stipulated for the jerk-limited stop, whose deceleration bound is $a_{\max} = a_{\text{brake}}$ (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Rack-end clear distance $D_{\text{clear}}$  | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["d_clear"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["d_clear"]`        | Clearance the stop must fit inside                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Total pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["tau_delay"]`      | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["tau_delay"]`      | Observation age, lease path, and brake onset (@sec-perception-latency-waterfall)                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Permission tick $T_{\text{tick}}$           | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_tick"]`         | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_tick"]`         | Period of the chosen permission-loop rate (@sec-nervous-cadences)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Chunk lease $T_{\text{lease}}$              | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_lease"]`        | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_lease"]`        | Longest an admitted chunk may drive without renewal (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing)                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Setpoint step $\Delta t$                    | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_step"]`         | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_step"]`         | Spacing of the chunk policy's setpoints (@sec-brain-action-chunking)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Chunk replan period                         | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_period"]`       | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_period"]`       | A whole number of setpoint steps                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Intent-model latency                        | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_intent"]`       | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_intent"]`       | Prefill plus decode on the application processor (@sec-brain-memory-wall)                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Intent-model rate                           | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["f_intent"]`       | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["f_intent"]`       | Largest rate whose period covers the latency                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| In-loop takeover $T_{\Sigma,1}$             | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_takeover_in"]`  | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_takeover_in"]`  | Slow-bound human reaction plus console video and handshake (@sec-intervention-reaction-drift)                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Out-of-loop takeover $T_{\Sigma,2}$         | `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_takeover_out"]` | `{python} MachineCard.category_str["t_takeover_out"]` | Take-over time of the 90th-percentile study condition plus video and handshake                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

: **The running machine's card**: The fifteen parameters of the warehouse mobile manipulator that later calculations use most. A derived value built on illustrative inputs is illustrative evidence. Values print from the MLSysIM registry when the book is built. {#tbl-01-machine-card tbl-colwidths="[24,12,12,52]"}

With the card fixed, every later design question about this machine starts the same way: identify which margin the intended action approaches, then establish the physical response available before that margin is exhausted. @Sec-body develops the force, heat, and power calculations. Whether a machine also needs the learning and delegated-authority discipline of this book is a separate question, which the scope test answers.

## The Physical AI Scope Test {#sec-boundary-scope-test}

A warehouse arm can follow a fixed control law, execute a human-approved offline path, or accept live learned proposals. All three can move the same hardware, but they place different obligations on the system. The scope test identifies the combination developed in this book.

The scope of physical AI is defined by the simultaneous intersection of three structural criteria (@fig-01-scope-venn):

1. **Learned Statistical Model:** The system relies on a policy, perception encoder, or world model whose behavior is specified by training data rather than by an inspectable requirement, such as a neural network or diffusion policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Evidence that such a component behaves correctly must therefore be gathered empirically over a stated operating domain. A linear plant model fitted by system identification, whose error bounds can be analyzed, does not meet this criterion; a neural policy does.
2. **Consequential Physical Feedback:** Actuator actions alter the material state of the physical environment, which in turn directly dictates what the sensors observe next under the governing laws of classical mechanics, thermodynamics, or electromagnetism.
3. **Delegated Physical Authority (System-Level Actuation):** A learned component's output, whether a percept, a state estimate, or a proposed action, can affect live actuation without synchronous human approval. The learned model need not write an actuator register itself; the system holds physical authority because that output can shape a command that reaches one. An automated check does not remove this authority, and a check that judges the command using the same learned perception is not independent of it: one perception error misleads the proposer and the check together.

::: {#fig-01-scope-venn fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and system-level authority to let learned outputs reach actuation without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control." fig-alt="Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and physical authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control."}
![](images/svg/fig01_scope_venn.svg){width="90%"}
:::

A classical proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller can regulate a motor through physical feedback without a learned component. Conversely, a learned market predictor can influence automated transactions without controlling the physical plant considered here. Neither satisfies all three criteria. This distinction identifies the engineering scope; it does not imply that either system is simple or harmless.

A learned model alone cannot define the field. An offline neural trajectory optimizer may compute paths for a manipulator, but if an engineer must inspect and explicitly load each path before execution, its outputs lack delegated runtime authority. A model that flags assembly defects on a display likewise leaves the physical decision to another actor. Conversely, many deployed machines are modular: learned perception feeds a planner written as rules or as an optimization. Such a machine meets the third criterion through its percepts, even though no learned component proposes motion; the Tempe vehicle in @sec-boundary-when-fails is one.

Shared autonomy belongs inside the scope whenever a learned component can affect live motion without approval of each correction. A hypothetical surgical assistant that applied learned haptic guidance could influence contact before the surgeon responds, even though the surgeon remains responsible for the overall task. No universal force threshold or human reaction time determines this classification. What matters is whether the automated system can execute the learned contribution.

Evaluating an ambiguous machine means testing each criterion independently, as the examples above do. A deterministic veto does not remove delegated authority; a mandatory human review of an offline plan does. When all three tests pass, the system operates as physical AI, and its engineering must respect the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {#chk-boundary-scope-test .callout-checkpoint title="Binding budgets and the scope test"}

- [ ] Can you explain why response delay and active braking consume separate portions of stopping clearance?
- [ ] Can you identify the relevant physical margins when the warehouse machine travels, presses a latch, and holds a load?
- [ ] Can you apply all three scope criteria to a new machine, including one whose learned output passes through an independent veto?

:::

The scope test establishes which responsibilities must be combined. The machine model places those responsibilities along the path from observation to physical action.

## The Machine in Five Levels {#sec-boundary-machine-model}

A machine that passes the scope test needs an organization that keeps its learned models from writing directly to the actuators they could damage, while still letting those models steer it.

The Body establishes what motion, force, and power the machine can sustain. The Brain supplies learned proposals within those limits. The Nervous System connects the two while preserving the time and authority needed to refuse an inadmissible proposal. The five-level model locates these responsibilities from learned computation down to the physical environment:

1. **The Brain (Level 1):** The learned models that interpret observations and propose goals or motion. A proposed sequence of future setpoints does not establish permission to execute the entire sequence.
2. **The Nervous System (Level 2):** The communication and control mechanisms that connect proposals to execution. Its permission path admits, modifies, or refuses proposals using current evidence and physical limits, and can initiate a feasible fallback without waiting for the proposer.
3. **The Body (Level 3):** The drives, transmissions, windings, structures, and power supply that deliver the admitted action.
4. **The Boundary (Level 4):** The interface where commands produce physical effects and sensors convert physical events into measurements.
5. **The World (Level 5):** Floors, payloads, contact, people, and other conditions that continue evolving whether the machine observes them or not.

One implementation places the learned proposer on an application processor, the permission path on a separate real-time controller, and the motor current loops on dedicated drives. The required separation follows from timing and fault assumptions; naming a processor family or operating system does not establish it. @Sec-nervous turns this division of responsibility into an explicit handoff record.

Governance is not a sixth level. It is the lifecycle envelope around all five, deciding who may command the machine, what evidence licenses it to operate, and when that license expires, and it changes on the timescale of interventions and releases rather than control cycles.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Transfers of command authority, and preemption of the proposal stream, are governed by the supervisor state machine in @sec-intervention-authority-transitions.
:::

::: {#dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary .callout-definition title="Proposal boundary"}

***Proposal boundary***\index{Proposal boundary!definition}\index{Permission path!definition} is the line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the **permission path**, an independent mechanism with bounded latency that the model cannot delay or corrupt and that alone may permit the action to reach an actuator. The permission path checks each proposal against fresh evidence, the stopping envelope, and a fallback feasible from the current state, and refuses when any check fails.

1.  **Significance**: Keeps model outputs from directly commanding actuators; the protection holds only while the permission path's sensing, physical limits, and fallback remain valid.
2.  **Distinction**: A policy that outputs torque values still has no actuator-write authority; its output is a proposal until the permission path admits it.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the permission path as a post-processing clamp on model outputs rather than an independent mechanism that can refuse execution when the proposer is late, wrong, or silent.

The proposal boundary governs who may authorize an action. The causal boundary is where the admitted command changes the plant. The Nervous System connects the two, checking proposals before allowing the drives to execute them.

:::

Readers from control will recognize a supervisory arrangement. The proposal boundary is a form of runtime assurance, whose Simplex architecture pairs a high-performance controller with a simpler verified one and a rule that decides which may drive the plant [@sha2001using]; @sec-enforcement develops it for this machine, and @tbl-01-law-lineage places the book's other terms in the field's vocabulary. Independence also constrains the permission path's evidence, not only its processor. If the path judges a proposal with the same learned perception that produced it, one perception error defeats both, so the sensing that grants permission must not share the learned component's failure modes (@sec-enforcement-where-enforcer-sits).

The margin stack that opens every chapter draws these same five levels (@fig-01-locator). The rates shown in the locator belong to the book's selected architecture; they are not universal requirements for each level. Later chapters derive the necessary timing from the task and body. For orientation, the essential feature is the proposal boundary between learned computation and execution authority.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-locator-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LOCATOR RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-01-locator (fig01_machine_levels.svg) in
# │          @sec-boundary-machine-model.
# │ Goal:    Keep the rates drawn on the Brain and Nervous System bands equal to
# │          the running machine's registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz; chunk renewal 20 Hz; setpoints 40 Hz; 1 kHz tick.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale. Nothing prints.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class LocatorRates:
    """Registry rates that fig01_machine_levels.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_step = (1 / RM.chunk_step).to(hertz).magnitude  # category: derived from the chosen step
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    drawn = {"intent": 2.0, "chunk": 20.0, "step": 40.0, "tick": 1000.0}  # labels in the SVG
    check(abs(f_intent - drawn["intent"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws intent at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk - drawn["chunk"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_step - drawn["step"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws setpoints at 40 Hz; registry says {f_step}.")
    check(abs(f_tick - drawn["tick"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws a 1 kHz permission loop; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # Guard-only class: it pins the values drawn in the figure; no prose outputs.
```

::: {#fig-01-locator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The five-level machine**: Each band carries its pinned rate and the chapters that work on it. The wider gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the proposal boundary, above which a component may only propose. A chapter-opening stack with no level highlighted marks a governance chapter. The permission-loop rate shown is one implementation." fig-alt="Five stacked horizontal bands labeled from top to bottom Brain (learned proposers, intent model 2 hertz, chunk renewal 20 hertz, setpoints 40 hertz), Nervous System (permission path, lease, fallback, a 1 kilohertz loop in one implementation), Body (drives, transmission, windings, rails, current loop 10 to 25 kilohertz), Boundary (register write and sensor capture, event-timed), and World (contact, friction, payload, people, continuous). A wider gap between Brain and Nervous System is labeled proposal boundary, above may only propose, below may command. A dashed outline enclosing all five bands is labeled governance, lifecycle envelope, Part IV, no control rate. Chapter numbers sit at the right edge of each band: Brain 3, 6, 8 to 11; Nervous System 4, 12, 13; Body 2; Boundary 1, 8; World 5, 7."}
![](images/svg/fig01_machine_levels.svg){width="100%"}
:::

A useful machine needs both capable proposals and a dependable execution path. The separation does not require refusing every imperfect proposal; a permitted correction can preserve task success while enforcing a physical limit. Performance evaluation must distinguish what the learned proposer accomplishes alone, what the whole machine accomplishes with normal corrections, and whether the protective response contains a hazard.

These responsibilities define the questions carried through the book. They also provide a way to analyze a failure without attributing every outcome to model accuracy.

## When the Responsibilities Fail Together {#sec-boundary-when-fails}

A warehouse model that recognizes an obstacle too late cannot recover the clearance already consumed. In a road vehicle, the same timing problem can combine with tracking errors, delayed intervention, and missing redundancy. The 2018 Tempe collision provides a documented example of these interacting failures; it does not establish that one prescribed hardware architecture would have prevented them. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) attributed the crash primarily to the vehicle operator's distraction. The design choices traced below explain why the automated system had made that single, unmonitored person the last line of defense.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-incident-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TEMPE AND CRUISE RECORDS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-law-lineage and @sec-boundary-when-fails (Tempe timeline,
# │          action suppression, braking cap, Cruise pullover, checkpoint).
# │ Goal:    Print the investigators' own values once, and derive the travel
# │          during action suppression from the two recorded speeds.
# │ Show:    5.6 s first detection; 43.2 mph at 1.2 s before impact; 1 s
# │          suppression ending at 0.2 s and 40.5 mph; takeover at 0.02 s;
# │          18.7 m during suppression; 7 m/s^2 (0.71 g) chosen cap against
# │          0.92 g (9.0 m/s^2) capability; Cruise about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up
# │          to 7.7 mph.
# │ How:     Literature values from NTSB/HAR-19/03 and the Quinn Emanuel report,
# │          loaded here until the literature registry holds them. Suppression
# │          travel uses the mean of the two recorded speeds (trapezoid rule);
# │          no counterfactual stop is computed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_math, check

class IncidentRecord:
    """Investigator-reported values for the Tempe (2018) and Cruise (2023) cases."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019), p. v and table pp. 15-16
    t_detect = 5.6 * second  # first detection, before impact
    t_recognize = 1.2 * second  # emergency recognized and suppression begins, before impact
    v_recognize = 43.2 * ureg.mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_suppress = 1.0 * second  # action-suppression period (p. 13)
    t_supp_end = 0.2 * second  # suppression ends, before impact
    v_supp_end = 40.5 * ureg.mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_takeover = 0.02 * second  # operator takes the wheel, before impact
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03, p. 13 and footnote 33
    a_cap = 7.0 * meter / second**2  # ADS emergency threshold and braking cap (chosen by the developer)
    g_capable = 0.92  # police-determined average deceleration capability in the crash area, in g
    # category: literature. Quinn Emanuel report to the Cruise boards (2024), p. 10
    d_drag = 20 * ureg.foot  # approximate distance moved during the pullover
    v_drag = 7.7 * ureg.mph  # maximum speed during the pullover

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    g0 = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)
    d_suppress = (0.5 * (v_recognize + v_supp_end) * t_suppress).to(meter)
    a_cap_g = (a_cap / g0).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_capable = (g_capable * g0).to(meter / second**2)
    d_drag_m = d_drag.to(meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs((t_recognize - t_supp_end - t_suppress).to(second).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Suppression must span the two table rows.")
    check(abs(a_cap_g - 0.71) < 5e-3, f"NTSB states the cap as 0.71 g, got {a_cap_g}.")
    check(a_capable > a_cap, "The chosen cap must sit below the vehicle's capability.")
    check(abs(d_suppress.magnitude - 18.7) < 0.05, f"Suppression travel is about 18.7 m, got {d_suppress}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_suppress_str = fmt_latency(t_suppress, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_recognize_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_recognize, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_supp_end_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_supp_end, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_takeover_math = fmt_math(rf"T-{fmt(t_takeover, unit=second, precision=2)}\text{{ s}}")
    v_recognize_str = fmt_velocity(v_recognize, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
    v_supp_end_str = fmt_velocity(v_supp_end, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
    d_suppress_str = fmt_length(d_suppress, unit=meter, precision=1)
    a_cap_str = fmt_acceleration(a_cap, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_cap_g_str = fmt(a_cap_g, precision=2)
    g_capable_str = fmt(g_capable, precision=2)
    a_capable_str = fmt_acceleration(a_capable, unit=meter / second**2, precision=1)
    d_drag_str = fmt_length(d_drag, unit=ureg.foot, precision=0)
    d_drag_m_str = fmt_length(d_drag_m, unit=meter, precision=1)
    v_drag_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
```

On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group's developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The vehicle carried lidar, radar, and cameras (@fig-01-tempe-vehicle). The ADS first detected the pedestrian `{python} IncidentRecord.t_detect_str` before impact, but detection alone did not provide a correct path prediction [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation]: **2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision**\index{2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision!NTSB report}: The event times and design details in this section come from NTSB highway accident report NTSB/HAR-19/03 [@ntsb2019uber].

### Tracking history loss under classification churn {#sec-boundary-tracking-churn}

Despite continuing to track the detected object, the ADS did not brake in response to it. The NTSB record shows classification changes among vehicle, bicycle, and other before `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

When the classification changed, the ADS path predictor did not use the object's earlier locations; for an "other" object it could assume a static path.[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking] The loss of earlier locations matters because successive positions provide evidence of motion across the roadway. A changing semantic label must not silently discard that evidence. The resulting path predictions did not place the pedestrian in the SUV's lane until `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking]: **Tracking History**\index{Tracking history!classification changes}: A path predictor can estimate motion from successive object locations. In the Tempe ADS, a changed classification caused the predictor to omit earlier locations; the NTSB report does not specify a Kalman-filter reset or a zero-velocity initialization [@ntsb2019uber].

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The stopping envelopes in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes bound what a classification change like Tempe's can cost.
:::

### Action suppression and the kinematic stopping deficit {#sec-boundary-action-suppression}

The ADS included an action-suppression interval intended to reduce responses to false alarms while the system checked the situation and allowed operator intervention [@ntsb2019uber]. That software choice also consumed time available for a physical response.

At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math`, with the vehicle traveling at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_recognize_str`, the ADS recognized an emergency and entered its one-second action-suppression period. The design withheld braking while it checked the hazard or waited for operator intervention. At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_supp_end_math`, suppression ended with the vehicle at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_supp_end_str`. The ADS then initiated a plan for gradual slowdown and sounded an alert; it did not request emergency braking. The NTSB notes that communication delay leaves unclear whether that slowdown began before the operator disengaged the ADS at `{python} IncidentRecord.t_takeover_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

The first term of the warehouse stopping budget applies directly. Averaging the two recorded speeds over the `{python} IncidentRecord.t_suppress_str` of suppression, the vehicle traveled about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` while emergency braking was withheld, distance that no later action could recover. The speed still fell during that second because a slowdown for the planned right turn at the next intersection was already under way; what the suppression withheld was the emergency response [@ntsb2019uber]. The emergency itself was defined by a chosen limit. The ADS treated a situation as an emergency when avoiding a collision required more than `{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_g_str` g) of deceleration or a jerk beyond its limit, and it capped its own automated braking at that deceleration; police determined that the vehicle could decelerate at an average of `{python} IncidentRecord.g_capable_str` g, about `{python} IncidentRecord.a_capable_str`, on that road surface [@ntsb2019uber]. The difference between a chosen permission limit and a physical one is the distinction the book's numbers keep throughout. We do not extend the calculation to a counterfactual stop, because the report does not establish when a different design would have begun braking. Detection, correct path prediction, hazard recognition, and physical braking are distinct events; reporting the first detection time alone conceals the failures between them.

::: {#fig-01-tempe-vehicle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Tempe test vehicle sensor locations**: The NTSB diagram identifies the developmental ADS vehicle's lidar, camera, radar, computing, and telecommunications locations. (Source: NTSB, public domain)." fig-alt="NTSB side-view diagram of the Volvo test vehicle with colored outlines marking lidar, cameras, radar, ADS computing and data storage, and GPS equipment."}
![](images/jpg/fig01_real_ntsb_tempe_vehicle.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {#ws-boundary-missing-safety-referee .callout-war-story title="The disabled safety redundancy (2018)"}
**Context**: On March 18, 2018, a developmental ADS on a 2017 Volvo XC90 struck and killed a pedestrian crossing a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].

**Mechanism**: As traced above, classification changes discarded the object's tracking history, and the one-second suppression withheld braking until only a gradual slowdown was planned. The design did not use maximum braking solely to mitigate an unavoidable collision [@ntsb2019uber].

**Impact**: The vehicle struck and fatally injured the pedestrian. The late gradual-slowdown plan could not recover the lost stopping opportunity.

**Response**: The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the vehicle operator's failure to monitor the driving environment and the ADS because she was visually distracted throughout the trip by her personal cell phone. It found three contributing factors at Uber ATG, all a consequence of an inadequate safety culture: inadequate safety risk assessment procedures, ineffective oversight of vehicle operators, and a lack of adequate mechanisms for addressing operators' automation complacency. The impaired pedestrian's crossing outside a crosswalk and the Arizona Department of Transportation's insufficient oversight of automated vehicle testing also contributed. The NTSB further found that deactivating the Volvo collision warning and automatic emergency braking, which Uber ATG had done over possible radar interference, removed a layer of safety redundancy, and it recommended stronger safety risk management for testing automated vehicles [@ntsb2019uber].

**Systems lesson**: Classification uncertainty, a delayed response rule, and reliance on an inattentive operator can combine. The design made the operator the primary countermeasure in an emergency, yet no mechanism monitored her attention in real time: authority rested on evidence nobody collected. A design needs timely hazard assessment and a response that can mitigate impact when avoidance is no longer possible; the investigation does not prescribe a particular processor or mailbox architecture.
:::

The investigation supports a broader architectural requirement. A developmental ADS needs safety redundancy and a timely mitigation path even when perception or path prediction fails, and simulation tests by Volvo that the NTSB cites suggest that the factory emergency braking might have prevented or mitigated this collision. The report does not establish when a separate permission path would have triggered or where it would have stopped the vehicle.[^fn-std-safety-standards]

[^fn-std-safety-standards]: **Safety-Critical Standards**\index{Safety-Critical Standards!autonomous systems}: Functional safety and intended-functionality standards can inform the safety case for sensing, actuation, and fallback. Their applicability and required implementation depend on the system and jurisdiction; the NTSB Tempe report did not mandate an isolated microcontroller architecture. @Sec-release-safety-cases-claims maps the standards that govern the running machine.

Tempe illustrates failure *before* impact, where classification changes and a software suppression delay prevented timely braking. The 2023 Cruise robotaxi incident marks the opposite pole *after* impact. A hit-and-run driver's car threw a pedestrian into the path of the driverless vehicle, which braked hard but struck her and stopped. It then began a pullover toward a minimal-risk condition and, because its sensing did not detect a person beneath the vehicle, moved about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_m_str`) at up to `{python} IncidentRecord.v_drag_str` while she was pinned beneath it. This account comes from a review commissioned by the company's boards, whose focus was the company's disclosures to regulators [@quinnemanuel2024cruise]; @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder analyzes the fallback.

Neither failure reduces to an inaccurate model. The first spent stopping distance before braking began, and no later action could recover it. The second chose motion after the impact. Together they show what must hold before the machine acts and what a fallback may do once harm has begun. Both also had to be reconstructed afterward from records of what the machine perceived and when, so accountability, like safety, depends on the path that authorizes motion.

::: {#chk-boundary-forensic-failure .callout-checkpoint title="Forensics of boundary and authority failures"}

Verify how the Tempe mechanisms connect to the architecture:

- [ ] **Classification changes and path prediction**: Can you explain how classification changes caused the ADS path predictor to omit earlier object locations, despite continued tracking?
- [ ] **Software suppression vs. kinematic clearance**: Can you distinguish the `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` recognition time from the one-second suppression period and explain why the gradual-slowdown plan at `{python} IncidentRecord.t_supp_end_math` could not restore the time already spent?
- [ ] **Safety redundancy**: Can you explain why disabling factory collision warning and emergency braking removed a layer of protection from a developmental ADS?

:::

## Safety Convergence {#sec-boundary-safety-convergence}

A robot approaching the end of an aisle needs a valid stopping decision whether its camera is dirty, its observations have been manipulated, or its model has made an ordinary prediction error. Safety concerns the resulting physical harm; security concerns deliberate interference; accountability concerns the evidence needed to explain the decision. These responsibilities intersect where the system authorizes motion.

For an ordinary failure, consider traction falling below the value assumed in the stopping calculation. The previous clearance bound may no longer support the same speed. Detecting that change and restricting operation requires evidence about the plant and environment, not merely confidence in the model's proposed path.

An adversary can instead target the evidence used to authorize motion. Corrupted observations or unauthorized command changes can alter a physical decision even when the model runs correctly. Independence from the proposer alone does not establish trustworthy sensing or authorized requests.

A valid credential establishes who may request an action, but not whether that action is physically admissible now. The same joint command can be acceptable far from a hard stop and inadmissible near it. **Physical authority is state-dependent.** Admission must consider current motion, load, temperature, and uncertainty, together with a response that remains feasible if operation cannot continue.

Accountability requires records that connect the decision to its physical outcome. The engineer needs to reconstruct the proposal, the state estimate and limits used to judge it, the admitted command, and the observed response. The records also need timing information precise enough to establish which evidence was available when the decision occurred. Recording a command does not prove that the actuator executed it, so command and feedback evidence serve different roles. Later chapters develop these records alongside the mechanisms they describe.

Safety, security, and accountability therefore ask the same three things of the permission path that guards the causal boundary: state fresh enough to judge the command, authority to refuse it, and a record of what was proposed, what was admitted, and what was written. The permission path is one part of a larger engineering task: choosing a useful physical capability, developing the learned behavior that supplies it, and integrating a machine that can deliver it under justified operating conditions.

## The Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-boundary-bedrock-laws}

Opening a door and carrying a load require more than a sequence of accurate predictions. The machine must respect its body's limits, learn from experience changed by its own actions, and connect proposals to justified execution. Four bedrock laws organize these responsibilities, each leading a part of the book.

**The first law: irreversibility.** Software rollback cannot undo physical consequences. The checks needed to admit an action must finish before that action consumes the available margin. The stopping calculation already showed why: delay spends clearance, and braking then needs additional distance. Reversing a command may recover a position, but it cannot repair a damaged object or erase heat already dissipated. Part I turns this distinction into physical budgets for the body and timing requirements for its controllers.

**The second law: endogenous data.** A physical agent's actions influence its future observations. A grasp changes the object's pose, and a poor approach can move the machine into states absent from its demonstrations. Single-step prediction accuracy therefore does not establish closed-loop competence. Part II develops collection, training, and evaluation as an improvement cycle: identify a failed behavior, gather suitable new experience, train a candidate, and test both its gains and regressions. Current evidence bounds the current claim; qualified new experience can expand it.

**The third law: proposal is not permission.** A learned model may propose; an independent permission path decides whether the proposal may execute. That decision requires sufficiently fresh state, applicable physical limits, and a feasible fallback when a proposal is late, absent, or inadmissible. Independence must hold under the stated timing and fault assumptions: the proposer must not be able to delay or corrupt the mechanism responsible for refusal. Part III builds the runtime around this separation of authority.

**The fourth law: evidence bounds authority.** Permission to operate depends on evidence for stated conditions. A successful demonstration does not establish safe behavior for every payload, sensor fault, or surface. The release argument must identify the supported operating domain, the assumptions behind its limits, and the conditions that require restricted operation or withdrawal. Tempe showed the violation: the design made one operator the primary countermeasure without monitoring whether she was attending. Part IV develops command authority, fault testing, and release decisions so that uncertainty limits what the machine is allowed to do.

Only the first law is physical. Irreversibility follows from the mechanics of work done on a plant, and no design choice relaxes it. The other three are design principles: engineering commitments the field has learned, often from accidents, that a team could choose to violate at a cost. We call all four laws because the book treats them as non-negotiable for the machines in its scope, but the distinction matters when a reader meets a design that seems to break one. None of the three principles is new. Each already has an established name and a canonical source, and @tbl-01-law-lineage maps the book's vocabulary onto them, together with the documented failure each distills, among them the Tempe and Cruise cases examined above. Where the book's term adds precision, as when it ties fresh evidence to a stopping budget, the book keeps its own name; the field's name remains the better term for searching the literature.

| Book's law or term                                                         | Kind             | Established name in the field                                             | Canonical source                                               | Documented failure it distills                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| Second law: endogenous data                                                | Design principle | Covariate shift; compounding error in imitation learning                  | Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell [@ross2011reduction]                 | A learning result rather than an accident: a cloned policy's errors can compound with the task horizon (@sec-data-covariate-shift)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

Only the first law is physical; the other three are design principles, which is why each has a literature of its own. {#tbl-01-law-lineage tbl-colwidths="[20,10,20,16,34]"}

The proposal boundary joins the four laws. Irreversibility requires checks before consequential action; endogenous data limits what training alone establishes; and evidence bounds the conditions under which admission is justified. More capable models do not remove these obligations. General methods can benefit from increased computation [@sutton2019bitter], but onboard computation still consumes memory bandwidth, energy, and cooling capacity. This book calls those constraints the **physical wall**\index{Physical Wall}; @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline measures their effect on the proposers. A refusal must also have a physical meaning: terminating computation does not stop a moving machine, so the runtime needs a timely response that the body can execute.

## The Architecture of This Book {#sec-boundary-book-architecture}

The book develops the ability to carry a learned proposal from a physical requirement to justified operation. The engineer first bounds what the machine can do, then establishes what its learned proposer has demonstrated, builds the runtime that checks live proposals, and tests the conditions under which operation may continue. Each part is led by one of the four laws. The records in @fig-01-spine preserve the assumptions and results of this reasoning so that later decisions can use them. One strand carries physical limits and evidence of competence; another carries the current observation and proposed action. They meet at the permission decision. @Sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis returns to the resulting engineering capability and the premises on which each claim depends.

A record is a machine-checkable statement that a later decision may rely on, and the stopping calculation (\ref{nbk-boundary-stopping-budget}) already has the shape of the first one, a limit record with the six elements set out in @sec-reader-numbers. Its value is the derived stopping distance. Its conditions are the loaded mass, a dry floor, a stationary obstacle, and a steady initial speed. Its uncertainty is not yet established, because every input is illustrative, and so its margin is not yet a margin: the spare distance is a difference between illustrative numbers. It has no detector, since nothing on the machine yet notices when the floor or the load leaves the stated conditions; @sec-body and @sec-enforcement supply one. Its provenance is the category label on each input. The empty entries are the point: a calculation becomes evidence only when every element is filled, and each box in @fig-01-spine is a record of this kind for a different decision.

::: {#fig-01-spine fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The spine of the book**: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except @sec-brain produces a record that a later one consumes. The lower row, in the Part III band labeled Proposal is not permission, runs observation contract 8, belief record 9, intent lease 10, and trajectory record 11. Both rows converge on the enforcement record of Chapter 12, which feeds the placement record of Chapter 13.
