A separate arrow runs from the evaluation record around the top and right edges to the release manifest."}
![](images/svg/fig01_book_spine.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Part I, The Machine Anatomy, turns irreversibility into design limits. @Sec-body measures the plant's budgets, @sec-brain establishes what the learned proposer can supply on time, and @sec-nervous connects them through a permission path whose timing follows from those budgets. The limit and handoff records make those assumptions explicit. Part II, Teaching the Machine, follows the consequences of actions changing future observations. @Sec-data, @sec-training, and @sec-evaluation develop the evidence needed to collect demonstrations, train a policy, and assess its competence within a declared operating domain. The demonstration provenance record, policy manifest, and evaluation record preserve both the supported claims and their gaps.

Part III, Running the Machine, implements the distinction between proposing and permitting an action. @Sec-perception through @sec-placement follow a command from a timestamped observation through a belief, an intent lease, and a proposed trajectory to admission and timely execution. Part IV, Governing the Machine, determines how evidence limits continued operation. @Sec-intervention, @sec-verification, and @sec-release address command authority, fault tests, and release conditions. @Sec-frontier concludes by applying the method to an unfamiliar machine, synthesizing what an engineer can now build and justify, and identifying the work needed to extend that capability. Across these parts, the warehouse mobile manipulator introduced here gives the reader one machine on which to connect the decisions. Its records make the reasoning inspectable; completing a record does not establish that the machine satisfies the physical claim it contains. The record register in @sec-appendix-systems-record-register gives each of the fifteen records its name, the chapter that produces it, and what it binds, and the machine card in @sec-boundary-running-machine fixes the machine's own parameters.

The route is a method for making useful behavior dependable. Four common misconceptions work against it from the start.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-boundary-fallacies-pitfalls}

Each misconception below imports an assumption that holds for software, for offline learning, or for classical control into a machine whose learned proposals can reach an actuator. The first assumes that training can do the permission path's work, and the other three assume that a human can intervene instantly, that latency only degrades performance, or that physical work can be undone.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Safety constraints can be trained into the policy.*

Learning pipelines often try to make a policy safe by penalizing undesirable behavior during training. Such objectives can reduce undesirable behavior on the training distribution, but that alone does not establish a bound on every command the deployed policy emits. Under novel sensor noise, a lens occlusion, or an out-of-distribution combination of states, nothing in the offline objective prevents an unsafe command. A training incentive shapes a probability distribution, whereas a stopping envelope requires a bound that holds on every cycle. The constraint therefore belongs downstream of the model, as a gate between the policy output and the actuator registers, which is where the third law places the permission path.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating human supervisory intervention as instantaneous in shared-autonomy systems.*

Consider a hypothetical surgical tool that applies haptic guidance force feedback from a learned anatomical model while a surgeon holds the instrument. Human supervision does not remove delegated authority during the interval before the surgeon can respond. If an actuator builds force before the operator can respond, its commands can deform tissue before the operator corrects them. The engineering question is how much force the system can apply during that interval. Local force limits enforced by the permission path must constrain the actuator without depending on either a timely neural prediction or an immediate human response.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming software latency merely degrades performance gracefully.*

A stalled proposer becomes dangerous if its last command remains active beyond the conditions supporting it. Execution therefore needs a bounded lifetime and a feasible response when that lifetime ends. Refusing an invalid replacement need not cancel an active command that remains valid, but it cannot extend that command's authority. An independent permission path can make a proposer stall a loss of availability rather than a loss of protection, only while its own evidence, timing, power, and fallback premises hold.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming physical actuation is reversible through subsequent software compensation.*

A manipulator applies excessive torque to a delicate fixture. Its monitor detects the anomaly after contact and reverses the motor command. Reversing a command cannot restore a fixture that has already plastically deformed or recover the energy already dissipated as physical heat in the motor windings ($I^2 R$). Detection can limit further damage, but it cannot erase the intervening physical work. The control architecture must therefore check commands against force and motion limits before execution. Recovery remains necessary, but it complements preventive enforcement rather than replacing it.

:::

## Summary {#sec-boundary-summary}

Physical AI joins two long lines of engineering, robotics and machine learning, and its history moves the learned model step by step toward the actuator. The causal boundary connects an admitted command to a physical effect. Restoring a software state cannot undo that effect; recovery requires another feasible physical response. A moving machine also travels while computation proceeds, so the chapter's timing and authority requirements place admission checks before consequential action. The warehouse example and the Tempe analysis show why prediction quality must be considered together with response time and available stopping clearance. The proposal boundary answers with an independent permission path, and four laws, one physical and three design principles, organize the book around it.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering across the causal boundary"}
* **Useful behavior needs a complete machine**: Physical AI combines learned behavior, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority. Designing it requires connecting task competence to the body, runtime, and evidence supporting operation.
* **Response delay spends physical margin**: The elementary budget $d_{\text{stop}} = v\tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2/(2a_{\text{brake}}) \le D_{\text{clear}}$ splits a stop into travel during the delay and travel while braking; below the crossover speed $v^{*} = 2a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}}$ the delay dominates, above it braking does. In the illustrative warehouse calculation, pre-brake travel adds `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_share_str` to braking distance. The relevant delay belongs to the path that produces the response, which can be independent of the learned proposer's completion time.
* **Proposal and permission have different jobs**: The Brain proposes useful actions; the permission path admits, modifies, or refuses them under current conditions. Its protection depends on valid evidence, physical limits, timing, and a feasible fallback.
* **Evidence guides improvement and operation**: Four laws lead the four parts. Only the first, irreversibility, is physical; endogenous data, proposal is not permission, and evidence bounds authority are the field's covariate shift, runtime assurance, and assurance-case disciplines, applied to one machine. The four parts connect machine anatomy, learning, execution, and governance. Their purpose is both to establish useful service under stated conditions and to identify the experiments or design changes needed to extend it.
:::

The engineer's task is to make the machine perform a useful physical task within its limits. That requires learned behavior suited to the task, timely computation, and a body able to deliver the requested motion. An independent permission path constrains execution even when the proposer is unavailable, subject to valid sensing, physical limits, and a feasible fallback. The next step is to establish those limits for the body that will carry out the action.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From the causal boundary to physical limits"}
A permission decision needs a physical limit against which to judge the proposed action. @Sec-body begins Part I by deriving stopping, actuator, thermal, and electrical budgets and examining how to measure them under stated operating conditions. Those measurements enter the limit record. @Sec-brain then examines the learned proposer's capabilities and timing, and @sec-nervous uses both sets of constraints to design the handoff and independent permission path. The progression starts with what the machine can sustain and ends with how computation may safely request it.
:::
